MOLT: A Fine-Grained GPU Memory Sharing System for LLM Serving with Opportunistic Fine-Tuning

Jaehoon Yang Affiliation: Seoul National University, Seoul, Republic of Korea email: jaehoon.yang@snu.ac.kr , Yongbeom Kim Affiliation: Seoul National University, Seoul, Republic of Korea email: kybs0627@snu.ac.kr , Hojoon Kim Affiliation: Seoul National University, Seoul, Republic of Korea email: hojoon.kim@snu.ac.kr , Seung Yul Lee Affiliation: Seoul National University, Seoul, Republic of Korea email: triomphant1@snu.ac.kr and Jae W. Lee Affiliation: Seoul National University, Seoul, Republic of Korea email: jaewlee@snu.ac.kr
Abstract.

Large language model (LLM) serving scales its replica count with the request load, yet GPU memory still stands idle inside the replicas. Adding a replica takes minutes, while the memory that a replica needs changes within seconds. Even instant autoscaling could not return this idle memory, because the smallest unit that it can remove is a whole replica. Colocating parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) with inference can use this memory, but inference must be able to reclaim it within seconds, before requests that wait for memory exceed their latency service-level objective (SLO). Existing colocation systems either keep the tuning memory resident or let inference reclaim it at the coarse granularity of a whole training sample. Each such reclamation also discards the running tuning step. To address these limitations, we present MOLT, a fine-grained memory sharing system that lets inference reclaim the memory of individual activations that a running tuning step has saved for its backward pass. The step continues, and its backward pass recomputes those activations. Inference reclaims only memory that no in-flight GPU work can still access, even under CPU–GPU asynchrony and tensor parallelism. On four model deployments (24B–70B) across H100 SXM and B200 GPUs under trace-driven workloads, MOLT keeps inference SLO attainment at or above 99.7% and completes 1.9–3.3×\times the tuning work of discard-based memory sharing.

1. Introduction

Request load in large language model (LLM) serving fluctuates heavily. Provisioning enough GPUs to meet the latency service-level objective (SLO) at peak load leaves them underutilized the rest of the time, so production systems autoscale. They add and remove replicas, each an independent serving instance that holds one copy of the model on one or more GPUs, as the load changes (Google Cloud, 2026a; Google Cloud, 2026b). Autoscaling follows the slow part of this fluctuation well, the daily cycle in which user-facing services peak during working hours and fall at night (Wang et al., 2025a; Stojkovic et al., 2025), and removes the capacity that a lower load leaves idle (Jaiswal et al., 2025). The fast part of the fluctuation, however, outpaces autoscaling, since the key-value (KV) cache of a replica, which dominates its dynamic memory use, can grow 3.2×\times within ten seconds while bringing up a replica and loading the model takes up to several minutes (Stojkovic et al., 2025). Each replica must therefore keep headroom to absorb the load that arrives before new replicas come up. One production autoscaler targets 60% GPU utilization by default, leaving each GPU idle 40% of the time (Google Cloud, 2026b). A deployment thus runs at an autoscaling floor, the fewest replicas that keep this headroom, where GPU compute and memory stay idle even with autoscaling. This memory cannot be returned to the provider, because a replica is withdrawn only as a whole.

Colocating another workload with inference can put this idle capacity to use. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) is a natural candidate. It is the standard way to adapt a deployed model (Han et al., 2024), and demand keeps growing, with Hugging Face hosting 256,295 PEFT adapters published at a rising rate since 2024 (He et al., 2025). It also fits colocation well. PEFT freezes the pretrained weights and trains only a small adapter (Hu et al., 2022), so when applied to the model that inference is serving it reuses the weights resident on the GPU. Its progress is measured in throughput rather than latency, so it can yield memory to inference during a burst and take it back afterwards.

Existing colocation systems dynamically share either the compute or the memory of the GPU. LLMStation (He et al., 2025) shares compute by interleaving tuning operations with inference iterations, but its tuning memory stays resident. Memory, however, is what determines whether inference meets its SLO during a burst. Inference admits a request only when the KV cache has room for it (Kwon et al., 2023; Yu et al., 2022), so a shortage of memory delays admission and lengthens the time to first token (TTFT). Likewise, a running request whose KV cache cannot grow for lack of memory stalls until memory frees up (Kwon et al., 2023; Sun et al., 2024). SIRIUS (Wang et al., 2025b) focuses on sharing memory, treating the training batch as elastic. When inference needs memory, it aborts the running step, restarts it with a smaller batch, and hands the freed memory to inference in a handover fast enough for the SLO. The memory boundary between the two workloads thus moves at runtime.

SIRIUS uses the idle memory that autoscaling removes, the memory a fixed number of GPUs leaves free as the load changes over minutes and hours. At the autoscaling floor, however, resizing the training batch moves the boundary in increments too coarse and at a cost too high. First, the smallest increment is one training sample, whose memory is large relative to the idle memory. A one-sample Mistral-Small-24B-Instruct tuning step at 1024 tokens holds 15.8 GiB beside the frozen weights, against 20–31 GiB idle on one H100. Tuning halts once the idle memory cannot hold one sample. Second, each handover discards the running tuning step and restarts it with a smaller batch, losing the work already done (Figure 1(a)). At the floor, this cost recurs whenever the KV cache outgrows the free memory, which happens within seconds.

Avoiding both limitations requires a unit of memory finer than a training sample, one that inference can reclaim without discarding the running step. We observe that the saved activation is such a unit. A saved activation is a tensor that the forward pass keeps for the backward pass to compute gradients. Saved activations hold most of a PEFT step’s memory (Liao et al., 2023) and can be recovered by recomputation (Chen et al., 2016; Jain et al., 2020; Kirisame et al., 2021). When inference reclaims the memory of some of them, the step continues, and its backward pass recomputes them (Figure 1(b)). Recomputation itself is well studied, but activation checkpointing fixes its memory budget before tuning starts. Here, the budget must change during the step, whenever inference reclaims memory.

Based on this observation, we present MOLT, a fine-grained memory sharing system that lets inference reclaim memory from a running tuning step one saved activation at a time. MOLT places the KV cache and the saved activations in one shared pool of physical GPU memory, and binds each saved activation to a fixed virtual-address range, called a slot. A slot is backed while physical pages of the pool are mapped behind it. When the KV cache needs more memory than the pool has free, MOLT unbacks slots and hands their pages to the KV cache while the tuning step continues. We call this mechanism continuous memory handover .

Handing memory over inside a running step raises two challenges. First, the tuning step must remain correct although its slots can be unbacked at any point. With flexible activation checkpointing , MOLT checks whether a slot is backed before each kernel that uses it, saves activations only into backed slots, and recomputes every activation whose slot is unbacked. Second, a handover must never unback a slot that GPU work may still access. Because the CPU dispatches kernels ahead of the GPU (NVIDIA Corporation, 2026a), a kernel dispatched several layers earlier may still access a slot when a handover arrives. With asynchronous-aware slot protection , MOLT protects every such slot, limits how far CPU dispatch runs ahead to keep the protected slots few, and makes every rank of a tensor-parallel deployment unback the same slots.

We evaluate MOLT on four model deployments (24B–70B) across H100 SXM and B200 GPUs under trace-driven workloads, where it keeps inference SLO attainment at or above 99.7% while tuning continues. Colocation that shares only compute reaches an SLO attainment of at most 5.0%. Against the discard-based memory sharing of SIRIUS, which also lets inference reclaim memory, MOLT completes 1.9–3.3×\times the tuning work. On both Mistral-Small-24B-Instruct deployments, MOLT with step-level handover, which moves the boundary only between steps, attains the SLO less often and completes less tuning work, which shows that the gain comes from the finer granularity rather than from the implementation.

In summary, this paper makes the following contributions:

  • •

    We identify the GPU memory that autoscaling leaves idle in LLM serving, and show that existing memory sharing cannot use it, because its unit, one training sample, is too coarse and each handover discards the running tuning step.

  • •

    We propose MOLT, a fine-grained memory sharing system whose continuous memory handover lets inference reclaim memory from a running tuning step one saved activation at a time.

  • •

    We design flexible activation checkpointing, which keeps the tuning step correct, and asynchronous-aware slot protection, which makes each handover safe under CPU–GPU asynchrony and tensor parallelism.

  • •

    We evaluate MOLT against compute sharing, discard-based memory sharing and MOLT with step-level handover, and show that it sustains inference SLO attainment while completing more tuning work than discard-based memory sharing.

2. Background

2.1. Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning

A deployed model is adapted continually (He et al., 2025; Shi et al., 2025), and PEFT is how that adaptation is done (Houlsby et al., 2019; Li and Liang, 2021; Lester et al., 2021; Hu et al., 2022). PEFT freezes the pretrained weights and trains a small set of added parameters, an adapter, which is why it has become the standard method for adapting large models (Han et al., 2024; Dettmers et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2024; Sheng et al., 2024). Hugging Face carries 256,295 repositories tagged as PEFT adapters, created between December 2023 and September 2026, and adapter publication has been rising since 2024 (He et al., 2025). Llama models alone account for 37,606 of them (Grattafiori et al., 2024).

PEFT reads the pretrained weights but never writes them. LoRA, its representative method, replaces the update to a weight matrix W∈ℝd×kW\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times k} with a low-rank product (Hu et al., 2022),

h⁡(x)=W​x+Δ​W​x=W​x+B​A​x,h(x)=Wx+\Delta Wx=Wx+BAx,

where B∈ℝd×rB\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times r}, A∈ℝr×kA\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times k}, and r≪min⁡(d,k)r\ll\min(d,k). Training updates only AA and BB, about r⁡(d+k)r(d+k) parameters instead of d×kd\times k, and the gradients and optimizer state shrink with them. A single copy of the model can therefore be shared between an inference process and a tuning process, rather than each holding its own (Rajbhandari et al., 2020).

2.2. Idle GPU Resources in Autoscaled Serving

A serving deployment follows request load by autoscaling, adding and removing GPUs to hold a utilization or concurrency target (Google Cloud, 2026b; Google Cloud, 2026a; The KServe Authors, 2026; The Ray Team, 2026). Platforms set that target below full utilization, at 60% GPU utilization by default on one of them (Google Cloud, 2026b). The load moves slowly enough for this to work. Consecutive five-minute intervals of the BurstGPT trace (Wang et al., 2025a) differ in request rate by a median of 1.25×\times, and the rate steps between levels (Figure 2(a)). The variation that autoscaling absorbs is large. For instance, the load of user-facing services peaks during working hours and falls at night (Wang et al., 2025a; Stojkovic et al., 2025). Over a week, peak load exceeds mean load by 4.1×\times in BurstGPT, and by 1.7×\times and 3.0×\times in the conversation and code services of the Azure trace (Stojkovic et al., 2025).

Autoscaling cannot follow the memory inside a replica, because that memory changes within seconds and adding capacity takes minutes. The scaling decision itself is prompt (Google Cloud, 2026a; The Kubernetes Authors, 2026). What takes minutes is bringing up a replica, whose GPUs hold the model split by tensor parallelism (TP) (Shoeybi et al., 2019), and loading the model into it (Stojkovic et al., 2025; Fu et al., 2024; Jaiswal et al., 2025). When load falls, a replica that served a peak is kept for five more minutes by default (Google Cloud, 2026a; The Kubernetes Authors, 2026). In Figure 2(b), the KV cache of a Mistral-Small-24B-Instruct deployment covers 3.9–14.8 GiB over 227 s and can grow 3.2×\times within ten seconds.

Idle memory inside a replica cannot be returned to the provider, because scaling down removes a replica only as a whole, and its TP degree is fixed when it launches (Wu et al., 2024). A deployment runs the smallest number of replicas that meets the SLO at the peak of any rise in load that autoscaling cannot follow. At that autoscaling floor, capacity stands idle between peaks. One H100 running Mistral-Small-24B-Instruct holds 43.9 GiB of weights and leaves 20–31 GiB of its memory unused (Figure 2(b)). Under the heavier load of Figure 2(c), the KV cache needs 51 GiB against the 25 GiB one GPU can offer beside the weights. The replica therefore spans two GPUs, which offer 87 GiB, and each of them holds 32–44 GiB unused.

2.3. Inference-first Tuning Colocation

A second workload colocated with inference can use the memory idle at the autoscaling floor, but only until inference needs it again. When load rises, inference must reclaim that memory within seconds, before the arriving requests wait for it (Kwon et al., 2023; Yu et al., 2022). This move across the boundary between the two workloads is a handover. The second workload must therefore tolerate interruption and hold a small resident footprint, the memory that inference can never reclaim from it. PEFT meets both requirements (§2.1). Its progress is measured in throughput rather than per-request latency, so it tolerates interruption. It shares the frozen weights inference already holds, so its resident footprint is small.

One line of colocation work shares compute. LLMStation (He et al., 2025) decomposes tuning execution into fine-grained units and interleaves them with inference iterations, which protects serving latency while tuning runs. Sharing compute leaves the memory boundary fixed. As arrivals rise, the KV cache grows until it fills the memory that tuning leaves free, and TTFT exceeds the SLO once it does (Figure 3).

The other line shares memory. SIRIUS (Wang et al., 2025b) moves the boundary at runtime by resizing the training batch, removing samples when inference needs memory and adding them back once demand subsides. To make a handover fast enough for an inference SLO, it hands the freed pages straight to inference, bypassing the training framework’s caching allocator (Paszke et al., 2019). §3 examines whether a boundary that moves at the granularity of whole training samples can follow the KV cache at the autoscaling floor.

3. Motivation

3.1. Limitations of Existing Memory Sharing

SIRIUS uses the idle memory that autoscaling removes, not the memory autoscaling leaves behind. Its target is the memory a fixed GPU count leaves free. This memory is large, so the boundary can move at the coarse granularity of whole training samples. It is also long-lived, so inference rarely takes it back and handovers are rare. Neither property holds at the autoscaling floor, where the idle memory is smaller and inference takes it back within seconds (§2.2).

A first limitation is granularity. Within a batch, samples are independent, so adding or removing a whole sample cleanly adds or removes its memory. That memory is large relative to what the floor leaves idle. A Mistral-Small-24B-Instruct tuning step of one sample at 1024 tokens holds 15.8 GiB beside the frozen base weights (Figure 4), against the 20–31 GiB left idle on one H100 at the floor (Figure 2(b)). There is no setting below one sample, so tuning halts entirely once the idle memory cannot hold one.

A second limitation is the cost of the handover itself. SIRIUS reclaims memory by discarding the current tuning step and restarting it with a smaller batch, so a handover late in a step wastes every operation the step has performed. At the floor, the KV cache can grow 3.2×\times in ten seconds (Figure 2(b)), and each rise takes memory back from tuning. The cost of a discarded step is therefore paid at the rate the KV cache moves, not at the rate the day’s load changes.

3.2. Activation as the Unit of Memory Sharing

The limitations of SIRIUS point to two requirements for PEFT colocation. First, the sharing granularity must be much finer than a whole sample, so that idle GPU memory is used efficiently and tuning is not forced to halt the moment a single sample no longer fits. Second, a handover must preserve the progress of the running PEFT step rather than discard it, so that frequent handovers do not starve tuning.

The saved activation meets both. A saved activation is a tensor that the forward pass keeps for the backward pass to compute gradients. It is the only unit in a PEFT step that meets both requirements. Persistent state, namely the adapter parameters, gradients and optimizer state, must stay resident to preserve progress, and only 0.4 GiB of a step’s memory is persistent, at every input length (Figure 4). Intermediate tensors live too briefly for their memory to be reclaimed. Saved activations dominate the rest of the step’s memory and can be recovered by recomputation (Chen et al., 2016; Jain et al., 2020; Kirisame et al., 2021; Peng et al., 2020). An activation is a fine-grained unit, because each one is small and can be dropped individually, at per-layer or per-operator granularity, rather than a whole sample at once. It also preserves progress, because a dropped activation is recomputed in the backward pass, and a handover then costs only that recomputation rather than the work that the step has already performed.

3.3. Key Challenges of Fine-grained Memory Sharing

Using the saved activation as the sharing unit raises two challenges.

C1. Adapting execution to a dynamically changing saved-activation set. Because activations are dropped dynamically during the step, the backward pass cannot assume that a saved activation is still available. An activation may have been dropped at any point after it was produced, so reading it directly could lead to a memory fault. The system must therefore check, at each backward access, whether the activation is still in memory, and recompute it when it is not.

C2. Dropping activations safely during execution. The CPU decides which activations to drop, but it dispatches GPU kernels asynchronously and runs far ahead of the GPU execution (NVIDIA Corporation, 2026a; Paszke et al., 2019), so a kernel it launched several layers back may still be reading or writing the activations of its layer. Freeing that memory would corrupt the kernel’s work, and the CPU must protect the activations of every kernel it has launched but not seen complete (NVIDIA Corporation, 2026c), which shrinks the set it can drop. Under tensor parallelism, the CPU’s lead over the GPU differs across ranks, so an activation can be safe to drop on one rank but not on another. Every rank must nevertheless drop the same activations, because tensor-parallel ranks must execute the same operators. The system must therefore make that decision at an arbitrary handover point. Dropping an activation that an in-flight kernel may still access causes a memory fault in the tuning step, and protecting one that no in-flight kernel can access withholds its memory from inference.

4. MOLT

4.1. Overview

MOLT provides continuous memory handover, which allows inference to reclaim memory from a running tuning step at the granularity of a single saved activation. The tuning step continues across a handover, and its backward pass recomputes each activation whose memory was reclaimed, so no completed work is discarded.

MOLT is a fine-grained memory sharing system with three components (Figure 5). The inference-side allocator and the tuning-side allocator run inside vLLM and PyTorch, respectively (§5.1). Each saved activation is bound to its slot, and the slot state table (SST) records whether physical pages back each slot. The handover controller manages the shared pool, which is preallocated and holds the KV cache and the pages of backed slots, the only memory a handover moves. When the KV cache exhausts the pool’s free pages, the inference-side allocator requests pages over inter-process communication (IPC), and the handover controller unbacks slots and hands their pages to the KV cache.

With flexible activation checkpointing, MOLT ensures that a tuning step remains correct when its slots are unbacked mid-step (C1, §3.3). The tuning-side allocator reads a slot’s backing state from the SST before each kernel that produces or consumes the slot’s activation (§4.3). The activation is saved in the forward pass only if its slot is backed, and in the backward pass, it is read from its slot if the slot is backed and recomputed otherwise. Unlike prior recomputation schemes (Chen et al., 2016; Jain et al., 2020; Kirisame et al., 2021), MOLT decides which activations to recompute from backing state that changes whenever inference reclaims memory, while the step is still running.

With asynchronous-aware slot protection, MOLT ensures that a handover unbacks no slot that in-flight GPU work may still access (C2, §3.3). The SST sets a slot’s enqueued flag while a kernel that uses the slot has been dispatched but has not completed, and the handover controller unbacks only slots whose flag is clear on every rank (§4.4).

4.2. Shared Memory Pool

MOLT divides physical GPU memory into a reclaimable pool , the shared pool of §4.1, and a pinned pool for everything a handover does not move (Figure 6(a)). The pinned pool holds inference-side workspace and the frozen base-model weights, which inference and tuning read from the same physical pages. It also holds the LoRA parameters, gradients, optimizer state and intermediate tensors of tuning, and the activation of every unbacked slot, so each activation occupies exactly one pool. The pinned pool holds an unbacked slot’s activation only until its last use in the forward pass, and the backward pass recomputes it (§4.3).

MOLT represents the tuning budget as the set of backed slots (Figure 6(b)). It reserves each slot once, before execution, from an offline profile of activation sizes, because the execution order of a tuning step is stable (Huang et al., 2020; Peng et al., 2020; Rhu et al., 2016). Backing or unbacking a slot maps or unmaps the physical pages behind its fixed address range, so no activation is moved when the budget changes.

The SST records three values for each slot (Figure 5). The handover controller writes the backing state when it maps or unmaps the slot’s pages, and the tuning-side allocator reads it before each kernel that uses the slot (§4.3). The recomputation cost ranks the slots for unbacking and is fixed for each activation before execution (§4.3). MOLT never unbacks a slot whose activation cannot be recomputed, such as the input of a layer. The third value is the enqueued flag of §4.1, which keeps a handover from unbacking a slot that in-flight GPU work may still access (§4.4).

4.3. Flexible Activation Checkpointing

MOLT lets a handover take effect at any point of a running tuning step and keeps the step correct (C1). A handover consists of two decisions, the slot-unbacking decision of the handover controller and the allocation-path decision of the tuning-side allocator (Figure 7(a)).

When inference requests MM bytes (REQUIRE(M) in Figure 7(a)), the handover controller takes the slot-unbacking decision and unbacks slots until they cover MM bytes. It considers only evictable slots, which §4.4 leaves unprotected because no in-flight GPU work can still access them. Among the evictable slots, it unbacks the slots with the lowest recomputation cost first, because every unbacked slot adds recomputation to the backward pass.

The tuning-side allocator takes the allocation-path decision when it dispatches each operator that produces a saved activation. If the activation’s slot is backed, the activation follows the save-path (SAVE in the figure). The activation is allocated at the slot’s address in the reclaimable pool, where the backward pass reads it if the slot is still backed. If the slot is unbacked, the activation follows the recompute-path (RECOM in the figure). The activation is allocated in the pinned pool, freed after its last use in the forward pass, and recomputed in the backward pass (Chen et al., 2016; Jain et al., 2020; Kirisame et al., 2021; Korthikanti et al., 2023). The allocator reads the backing state again when it dispatches each backward operator, so an activation whose slot is unbacked after it was saved is recomputed as well.

In Figure 7(b), each row holds one kind of saved activation, each box is the slot of that activation in one layer, and SS is the recomputation cost of the row. Before the handover, every slot is backed. When the handover arrives, the CPU has dispatched the layers up to 5, but the GPU is still executing layer 3. In-flight GPU work may therefore still access the slots of layers 3 to 5, inside the box, so they are not evictable. The handover unbacks every other slot, so only these three layers keep backed slots. The activations that layers 0 to 2 have already saved are recomputed in the backward pass, and layers 6 onward allocate their activations in the pinned pool. With a smaller handover request, the handover controller would stop earlier, and it would unback the slots of the qkv_proj row first, because that row has the lowest SS.

Every operator dispatched after the handover follows the new backing state (Figure 7(c)). The handover controller only writes the backing state, and the tuning-side allocator reads it when it dispatches an operator. Layers 3 to 5 were dispatched before the handover, so their slots remain backed, and the operators of layer 5 follow the save-path, drawn in blue. Layer 6 is dispatched after the handover, when its slots are already unbacked, so its operators follow the recompute-path, drawn in red. In the backward pass, layer 6 comes first, and MOLT recomputes its activations before its operators run. The operators of layer 5 then read their activations from their slots.

Unlike discard-based handover, MOLT never restarts the step, and a handover costs only the recomputation of the activations whose slots it unbacks (Figure 8). Discard-based handover couples every memory-boundary change to aborting and restarting the running step (§3.1). In Figure 8(b), the forward work already done is discarded, and in Figure 8(c), it is kept and only the activations of unbacked slots are recomputed in the backward pass. Pages reach inference through the same handover path that discard-based systems use (Wang et al., 2025b).

Memory is handed back to tuning only at step boundaries, by re-backing unbacked slots. At the start of each step, the handover controller maps free pages of the pool behind unbacked slots again, highest recomputation cost first, and stops when the pool has no free pages left. The remaining unbacked slots wait for a later step boundary. Re-backing a slot in the middle of a step would spare recomputation only for activations that the step has not produced yet. Waiting for the next step boundary therefore costs at most the extra recomputation of the rest of the current step. Because re-backing discards nothing, MOLT re-backs at every step boundary at which the pool has free pages. A discard-based system instead waits until free memory exceeds a threshold, because it moves the boundary only at a coarse granularity (Wang et al., 2025b).

4.4. Asynchronous-aware Slot Protection

MOLT protects every slot that in-flight GPU work may still read or write, and a handover unbacks only the other slots (C2). Under TP, every rank must also unback the same slots (Figure 10). MOLT protects these slots without discarding the GPU work dispatched before the handover. MOLT classifies every slot by the enqueued flag that §4.1 defines. A slot is claimed while the enqueued flag of the slot is set. A handover leaves the backing state of a claimed slot unchanged, whether the slot is backed or was unbacked by an earlier handover. A slot is evictable when the enqueued flag of the slot is clear.

The set of claimed slots, the protection window, contains the slots of every layer from the layer before the completion frontier to the dispatch frontier (Figure 9(a)). The completion frontier is the layer that the GPU is executing, and the dispatch frontier is the last layer that the CPU has dispatched. The window includes the layer before the completion frontier because the first operators of a layer read the output of the previous layer. MOLT tracks GPU completion with a host-side callback, a CPU function that runs once the GPU has completed a layer (NVIDIA Corporation, 2026d). MOLT sets the enqueued flag of every slot of a layer when the CPU dispatches the first operator of the layer. The enqueued flag covers a whole layer rather than one operator, because a later operator of the same layer, such as a residual connection, may read a slot that an earlier operator wrote (Vaswani et al., 2017). MOLT clears the flag of a layer only when the host-side callback of the next layer runs. The dispatch frontier usually runs several layers ahead of the completion frontier, because CPU dispatch is asynchronous to GPU execution. In Figure 9(a), the CPU has dispatched layer 8 while the GPU still executes layer 1. The protection window thus contains layers 0 to 8, drawn in orange. The CPU has not yet dispatched layers 9 onward, whose slots are evictable and drawn in yellow.

When a handover request arrives, MOLT freezes the protection window until the handover controller has decided which slots to unback and has unbacked those slots. We call this mechanism the protection snapshot. Without the protection snapshot, the CPU could dispatch an operator that uses one of the slots to unback, and that operator would then access a slot that has no physical pages. The protection snapshot therefore pauses CPU dispatch and holds the dispatch frontier in place. The pause has little effect on tuning, because the GPU continues to execute the operators already dispatched. The protection snapshot also defers the host-side callbacks that would advance the completion frontier, and thereby keeps every slot of the protection window claimed until the slots to unback are decided. A slot may remain claimed slightly longer than necessary, but no slot becomes evictable too early. After the handover controller has unbacked the chosen slots, MOLT runs the deferred callbacks and resumes CPU dispatch.

MOLT keeps the protection window small by limiting how far CPU dispatch may run ahead of GPU execution, which leaves more slots evictable when a handover request arrives (Figure 9(b)). We refer to this mechanism as dispatch throttling. Without dispatch throttling, the protection window contains every layer that the CPU has dispatched ahead of the GPU, seven layers in Figure 9(a), and no slot in the protection window can be unbacked. MOLT enables dispatch throttling by modifying the software GPU kernel management technique used in SIRIUS (Wang et al., 2025b). The technique holds dispatched operators in a queue until the GPU executes the operators, and MOLT adds a dispatch cap on the number of operators in the queue. When the queue reaches the dispatch cap, CPU dispatch waits until the GPU has executed enough operators to bring the queue below a threshold, which we set to half of the dispatch cap. In Figure 9(b), CPU dispatch waits after each layer, and the gap between the dispatch and completion frontiers shrinks from seven layers to one.

MOLT chooses the dispatch cap by offline profiling, as the smallest dispatch cap that does not lengthen the tuning step. A larger dispatch cap only widens the protection window, and a smaller dispatch cap leaves the GPU waiting for the CPU. The chosen dispatch cap therefore keeps the protection window as small as possible without slowing tuning.

Under TP, each rank keeps a separate protection window, and the handover controller unbacks only slots that lie outside the union of the rank-local protection windows (Figure 10(b)). Collectives such as NCCL all-reduce (NVIDIA Corporation, 2026e) keep the GPUs of the ranks nearly aligned, but the dispatch frontiers of the ranks can differ (Figure 10(a)). In the figure, every GPU executes layer 3, but rank 0 has dispatched layer 6, rank 1 layer 5, and rank K−1K-1 layer 4. The slots of layer 6 are therefore claimed on rank 0 but evictable on ranks 1 and K−1K-1, and the slots of layer 5 are evictable only on rank K−1K-1, drawn in red. The collectives of the ranks would no longer match if every rank unbacked the slots that are evictable on that rank alone, because the ranks would then recompute different operators. The union of the rank-local protection windows, drawn in green, contains layers 2 to 6 on every rank. When a handover request arrives, every rank takes a protection snapshot and publishes the rank-local protection window through shared memory, and every rank then chooses the same slots to unback from the same union, without exchanging the chosen slots.

5. Evaluation

We evaluate MOLT in inference-first colocation, where tuning uses the GPU memory that inference leaves idle and inference reclaims it whenever the KV cache needs more. The evaluation answers three questions.

  1. (1)

    Does inference keep its SLO attainment while MOLT completes more tuning work than discard-based memory sharing (§5.2, §5.3)?

  2. (2)

    Is the gain caused by handover granularity rather than by the implementation that carries it (§5.2, §5.4)?

  3. (3)

    How much tuning speed does the dispatch cap cost, and how long does a handover delay inference (§5.5, §5.6)?

5.1. Experimental Setup

Hardware. We run Mistral-Small-24B-Instruct on 1×\timesH100 SXM and 2×\timesH100 SXM  (Choquette, 2023), and Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct on 4×\timesH100 SXM and 1×\timesB200  (NVIDIA Corporation, 2026f) (Table 1).

Models and adapters. We tune rank-8 LoRA (Hu et al., 2022) adapters on Mistral-Small-24B-Instruct (Mistral AI, 2025) and Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct (Grattafiori et al., 2024).

Datasets and traces. We use ShareGPT (sha, 2023) prompts for inference and the Alpaca (Taori et al., 2023) dataset for tuning. A tuning sequence has 768, 2048, 1024 and 512 tokens in the deployments of Table 1, respectively. Inference requests arrive according to the BurstGPT trace (Wang et al., 2025a).

Implementation. MOLT is implemented as a patch to vLLM v0.11.0 (Kwon et al., 2023) and an extension library for LLMStation’s build of PyTorch 2.8.0 (Paszke et al., 2019). The patch changes 2.7K lines in 23 of vLLM’s files and adds a 9.7K-line module. The module ports LLMStation’s execution interleaving (He et al., 2025) to vLLM’s V1 engine (vLLM Team, 2025) and integrates MOLT with it. The 13.1K-line library backs and unbacks slots through CUDA virtual memory management (NVIDIA Corporation, 2026b) on SIRIUS’s page pool (Wang et al., 2025b).

Baselines and ablation. We compare MOLT with continuous handover, the full design, against two baselines and one ablation. The ablation, MOLT with step-level handover, differs from MOLT with continuous handover only in when the boundary may move, so it isolates handover granularity. LLMStation-only shares only compute. It keeps tuning memory resident by excluding the same amount of memory from KV cache admission. LLMStation+SIRIUS also shares memory. At each handover, it resizes the training batch and discards the running step (Wang et al., 2025b). Its shared pool is the same size as that of MOLT. At each step boundary, MOLT with step-level handover reserves memory for inference. The reserve is the KV cache that the waiting requests need, multiplied by a reserve factor, plus a fixed margin. We report the factor with the highest SLO attainment among five factors from 2.0 to 4.0 (§5.4).

Metrics and SLOs. We report SLO attainment and tuning throughput over a measurement window. SLO attainment is the fraction of requests arriving in the window that meet the SLO (Li et al., 2023; Zhong et al., 2024). Tuning throughput is the number of tokens in the tuning samples completed in the window, per second. A request meets the SLO when its TTFT and its time per output token (TPOT) are each within 3×\times the mean for the same deployment running inference alone (Lee et al., 2025; Hong et al., 2025; Agrawal et al., 2024; Patel et al., 2024).

5.2. End-to-end Evaluation

MOLT with continuous handover is the only configuration whose SLO attainment and tuning throughput are both high on every deployment. In Figure 11, MOLT with continuous handover alone lies in the upper right on every deployment. The TTFT and TPOT percentiles in Table 2 are over the requests in the measurement window.

SLO attainment. MOLT with continuous handover meets the SLO for at least 99.7% of requests on every deployment, at the right edge of Figure 11, and LLMStation-only for at most 5.0%, at the left edge. LLMStation+SIRIUS also meets it for at least 95.5 %, because it also moves memory to inference at each handover. LLMStation-only keeps tuning memory resident, so requests wait for the memory that tuning holds (§2.3). The TTFT p50 of LLMStation-only is at least 6746.8  ms on every deployment, against at most 592.4  ms under MOLT with continuous handover (Table 2).

Tuning throughput. Of the configurations that meet the SLO, MOLT with continuous handover completes the most tuning work. It completes 1.9–3.3×\times the tuning work of LLMStation+SIRIUS on every deployment (Figure 11). The ratio is smallest on Mistral-Small-24B-Instruct at TP=1, 242.6 against 127.7 tokens/s, and largest on Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct at TP=4, 64.5 against 19.3 tokens/s (Table 2). At each handover, LLMStation+SIRIUS discards the running step, and MOLT with continuous handover preserves it. §5.3 counts the discarded steps. LLMStation-only tunes faster on both Mistral-Small-24B-Instruct deployments, at 285.1 and 606.1 tokens/s, because its tuning memory is never reclaimed.

Source of the gain. Handover granularity alone explains why MOLT with continuous handover outperforms MOLT with step-level handover on both Mistral-Small-24B-Instruct deployments. The two differ only in when the boundary may move (§5.1). On Mistral-Small-24B-Instruct at TP=1, MOLT with continuous handover meets the SLO for 99.7 % of requests at 242.6 tokens/s, against 69.0 % at 212.8 tokens/s for MOLT with step-level handover. At TP=2, MOLT with continuous handover also attains more and tunes faster. Its TTFT p95 at TP=1 is 619.7  ms against 3112.9  ms, and §5.3 shows where the requests of MOLT with step-level handover wait. On Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct at TP=4, the gap is in SLO attainment only. MOLT with continuous handover attains 99.7 % against 74.3 % at the same 64.5 tokens/s.

5.3. Memory Utilization

At the memory boundary, MOLT with continuous handover gives tuning most of the memory that inference leaves free, and inference rarely waits for memory. The end-to-end differences of §5.2 arise there. Figure 12 draws how inference and tuning divide the shared pool over the first 80 s of each deployment’s measurement window, on one time axis. The inference KV cache is drawn up from zero. The tuning-backed memory is drawn down from the pool size, which is dashed. A tick above the pool marks the arrival of each request that misses the SLO. Every configuration of a deployment ran at one pool size, so a row compares them on one memory axis. The percentages below are over the whole measurement window, and the attainable budget is the pool minus the inference KV cache.

Memory use. MOLT with continuous handover uses most of the attainable budget for tuning, and LLMStation+SIRIUS leaves most of it unused, in every row of Figure 12. On Mistral-Small-24B-Instruct at TP=1, MOLT with continuous handover backs 86% of the attainable budget on average, and MOLT with step-level handover backs 81%. In contrast, LLMStation+SIRIUS leaves 87% of that budget unused. MOLT with continuous handover unbacks slots within a step, and it re-backs them only at a later step boundary, because waiting costs at most the recomputation of the rest of the step (§4.3). In Figure 12, its tuning-backed memory therefore shrinks within a step as the KV cache grows, and grows back only at step boundaries. The tuning-backed memory of MOLT with step-level handover, however, changes only at step boundaries, in both directions. LLMStation+SIRIUS gives tuning a discarded step’s memory again only after free memory exceeds a threshold (§4.3), so it gives tuning either all of that memory or none of it. It discards 16.7% of its step attempts.

Waiting for memory. MOLT with continuous handover rarely makes inference wait for memory, and MOLT with step-level handover often does. We sample the inference engine’s request queue every 0.5 s. On every deployment, a request was waiting for memory in at most 1.4% of the samples under MOLT with continuous handover, against 27–47% under MOLT with step-level handover. Almost all SLO misses of MOLT with step-level handover exceed the TTFT limit, so its ticks in Figure 12 mark requests that waited for their first token. MOLT with continuous handover and LLMStation+SIRIUS both give inference memory within a step, and the handovers of MOLT with continuous handover give inference the requested memory within 1.6 ms at p99. MOLT with step-level handover gives inference memory only at step boundaries. A request whose KV cache does not fit in free memory therefore waits until the running step ends.

5.4. Granularity of the Memory Boundary

MOLT with continuous handover meets the SLO for more requests than MOLT with step-level handover at every reserve factor on every deployment (Figure 11). Only on Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct at TP=4 does a factor tune faster than MOLT with continuous handover. The factor sets how much memory MOLT with step-level handover reserves for inference at each step boundary (§5.1). On Mistral-Small-24B-Instruct at TP=1, the middle factor, 3.0, is the best on both axes, and Table 2 reports it. The other four attain as little as 43.1 %, and neither axis is monotonic in the factor.

MOLT with continuous handover moves the boundary far more often than MOLT with step-level handover, and no reserve factor removes the waits for memory that follow. On Mistral-Small-24B-Instruct at TP=1, MOLT with continuous handover handed memory to inference 194 times over each whole run, against 24 for MOLT with step-level handover at factor 3.0. Even at factor 3.0, a request was waiting for memory in 47% of the samples (§5.3). At the other four factors, this share is higher, at 54–64%.

5.5. Dispatch Throttling Analysis

A dispatch cap can leave most saved activations evictable without slowing tuning, on every deployment. The cap trades evictable memory against tuning speed (§4.4), and Figure 13 sweeps it on each deployment of Table 1. Each sweep runs tuning without inference at the deployment’s tuning sequence length. Evictable memory is the share of layers outside the protection window at its widest. Its base excludes the five layers that the backward pass keeps claimed at every cap, so it is 100% when the window is at its minimum. The point at ∞\infty is the unthrottled run, without a cap. Tuning speed retained is the tuning speed at the cap as a share of the unthrottled speed. The shaded band is ±\pm5% of the unthrottled speed, a tolerance we set rather than a spread we measured. Each point is one run. The dashed line marks the smallest cap from which no larger cap falls below the band.

At the dashed cap, tuning speed stays within the band, and the protection window at its widest spans 12.5, 12.5, 7.5 and 6.3% of all layers, close to its minimum, against 45, 65, 100 and 55% without a cap, in the order of Table 1. The dashed cap is 32, 64, 128 and 32. Tuning slows at the smallest caps. At a cap of 4, a step takes 13.1–24.6% longer than unthrottled.

5.6. Handover Overhead Analysis

A handover takes at most 1.3% of a tuning step, and only page allocation on the inference side grows with the handover size. A handover delays the inference request that needs its pages, from the page request of the inference-side allocator to the completion of page allocation. Under MOLT with step-level handover, that request waits instead until the running step ends (§5.3), so we state the latency as a share of a tuning step. In Figure 14, each bar is the mean latency of at least 19 handovers of one size, broken into four stages and Other, the time between them. In time order, the inference-side allocator requests pages over IPC (IPC request), and the handover controller takes the slot-unbacking decision and unbacks the chosen slots (Slot unbacking). The controller then acknowledges over IPC (IPC ack), and the allocator allocates their pages to the KV cache (Page alloc). At the largest size drawn for each deployment, 256, 128, 128 and 512 MiB in the order of Table 1, the mean handover takes 1.0, 1.3, 0.7 and 0.8% of a step.

Three stages change little with the handover size: the IPC request, slot unbacking and the IPC acknowledgment. They take 0.64–0.87 ms on the two deployments at TP=1 and 1.09–1.47 ms on the two with tensor parallelism, and they are more than half of a handover at the smallest size on every deployment. Of the three, slot unbacking grows the most with the tensor-parallel degree, yet it remains within 0.07% of a tuning step at every degree. It takes 0.05–0.12 ms at TP=1, 0.22–0.32 ms at TP=2 and 0.38–0.53 ms at TP=4. It grows because, under tensor parallelism, the slot-unbacking decision also waits for every rank’s protection snapshot (§4.4).

Page allocation changes little at small handover sizes and grows almost in proportion to the size at large ones. In Figure 14, on both deployments at TP=1, allocation remains within 0.44–0.72 ms up to 64 MiB per GPU. Beyond that size, each doubling of the size multiplies it by 1.5–2.0. The growth comes from allocation taking each page from the free list of the shared pool and zero-filling it. At TP=2, allocation grows from the smallest size drawn. At TP=4, it rises at 64 MiB, the first size measured with a longer interval between handovers.

6. Related Work

Colocation of LLM inference and tuning. Unlike prior colocation systems, MOLT reclaims memory from a running tuning step without discarding the step. FineInfer runs inference between tuning steps (He et al., 2024). FlexLLM interleaves tuning and inference tokens in each iteration and reserves the KV cache statically (Oliaro et al., 2026). LLMStation interleaves tuning operations with inference iterations while tuning memory remains resident (§2.3). SIRIUS moves the memory boundary by discarding the running step and restarting it with a smaller batch (§3.1). MOLT reuses LLMStation’s interleaving and SIRIUS’s page pool (§5.1), but its unit of memory sharing is a saved activation rather than a training sample.

Activation checkpointing. MOLT builds on activation checkpointing and differs from it in the memory budget, which inference changes while the tuning step runs (§4.1). Checkpointing chooses which activations to recompute under a budget fixed before training starts (Chen et al., 2016; Jain et al., 2020; Korthikanti et al., 2023; Gruslys et al., 2016). DTR and Capuchin decide at run time under such a budget (Kirisame et al., 2021; Peng et al., 2020). Like DTR (Kirisame et al., 2021) and selective recomputation (Korthikanti et al., 2023), MOLT gives up the activations that are cheapest to recompute first (§4.3). In these systems, the memory an activation gives up stays with the training job. In MOLT, inference reclaims it while dispatched kernels may still access it, which asynchronous-aware slot protection makes safe (§4.4).

7. Conclusion

Autoscaling leaves GPU memory idle inside LLM serving replicas, because it cannot follow a KV cache that changes within seconds and removes a replica only as a whole. Existing colocation systems either keep the tuning memory resident or let inference reclaim it only in whole training samples, discarding the running tuning step each time. We present MOLT, a fine-grained memory sharing system for colocating LLM inference and tuning. MOLT lets inference reclaim memory one saved activation at a time, safely under CPU–GPU asynchrony and tensor parallelism, while the running step continues and recomputes those activations. Experiments show that MOLT keeps inference SLO attainment at or above 99.7% while completing 1.9–3.3×\times the tuning work of discard-based memory sharing.

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.
